title: The resurrection of Jesus
note: The historical argument reasons abductively: certain facts about Jesus's death and its aftermath are granted by most critical historians, and the resurrection is claimed as their best explanation. Rivals include swoon, theft, wrong tomb, legend, and vision hypotheses. Hume's critique of miracle reports and the question of prior probability frame the whole debate.

read.title: Facts and their best explanation
text: Gary Habermas's minimal facts approach does not ask the skeptic to accept the Bible as inspired or even generally reliable. It uses only facts that are well evidenced and granted by the great majority of critical scholars, including skeptical ones. The argument is abductive:

(1) Jesus died by crucifixion. (2) Soon afterward his disciples sincerely believed that he had risen and appeared to them. (3) Paul, a persecutor of the church, came to believe the same. (4) James, Jesus's skeptical brother, came to believe the same. (5) The best explanation of these facts is that God raised Jesus from the dead.

Many defenders add the empty tomb, which a majority of scholars, though not all, accept. The creed Paul hands on in 1 Corinthians 15, which most date to within a few years of the crucifixion, lists appearances to Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred at once, James, and all the apostles; Paul then adds himself.
The leading naturalistic rival is the vision hypothesis, defended by Gerd Lüdemann: grief and guilt produced visions, first in Peter, then spreading to others.

Defenders reply that this fits the facts poorly. Visions are private, yet the creed reports group appearances. Paul and James were not grieving followers. And visions alone would not explain an empty tomb. Critics answer that any natural explanation, however strained, is more probable than a miracle; defenders reply that this depends on whether one has independent reason to think God exists.

q.q: What kind of argument is the minimal facts case?
Why are Paul and James a problem for the vision hypothesis?
On what, say defenders, does the 'more probable than a miracle' reply depend?
o: Whether one has independent reason to think God exists
